stories.headline: AI-CAPEX ROUT DEEPENS AS NASDAQ 100 SHEDS 3.48%, S&P DROPS 1.83%
stories.body: A day after Alphabet's post-earnings plunge, Amazon's results extended the hyperscaler selloff, dragging the Nasdaq 100 down 3.48% to roughly 28,385 and the S&P 500 off 1.83% to about 7,580 — the worst session of the week. Traders are now pricing a second straight quarter where AI capital spending outruns the revenue showing up to justify it.
stories.explain: When two of the index's largest cap-weighted constituents disappoint on the same metric — cloud growth versus capex — in back-to-back days, the market stops treating it as company-specific noise and starts repricing the whole AI-infrastructure trade at once, which is why the drawdown accelerated rather than stabilized. That kind of correlated, sector-wide repricing is exactly what shows up as a sharp one-day move in a cap-weighted benchmark, since the same handful of names that drove the index up on the way in are now driving it down on the way out.

stories.headline: GOLD TUMBLES 2.62% TO $3,899 EVEN AS STOCKS SELL OFF — A SIGN OF FORCED LIQUIDATION, NOT RISK APPETITE
stories.body: Spot gold fell nearly 3% to roughly $3,899 an ounce in the same session the S&P 500 lost 1.83% and the Nasdaq 100 lost 3.48% — an unusual pairing, since gold typically rallies when equities sell off. The move lines up more with funds raising cash to cover losses elsewhere than with a shift in investors' safe-haven preference.
stories.explain: Gold's normal role is a safe-haven hedge that gains when stocks fall, but that correlation flips during a 'dash for cash': when a leveraged portfolio takes losses on one asset, margin calls force the sale of whatever is most liquid and still has a profit cushion — often gold — regardless of that asset's own outlook. The same mechanism showed up in the 2008 crisis and March 2020, when gold fell alongside equities for days before resuming its traditional inverse relationship once the liquidity scramble eased.

stories.headline: 10-YEAR YIELD RETREATS TO 4.93% AS TREASURIES CATCH THE FLIGHT-TO-QUALITY BID GOLD DIDN'T
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield slipped about 6 basis points to 4.93%, pulling back from last week's push above 5%, as investors rotated into government debt rather than gold while equities sold off. The divergence — bonds rallying, gold falling — shows the flight-to-safety flow is going almost exclusively into Treasuries.
stories.explain: Falling yields mean rising bond prices, so the drop in the 10-year is the market's conventional safe-haven response to the equity selloff — investors bidding up government debt for its credit quality and liquidity. That Treasuries, not gold, are absorbing the flow confirms the gold decline is a liquidity-driven anomaly rather than a broad repricing of risk appetite, since the two assets are supposed to move together, not apart, in a classic flight to quality.

stories.headline: WTI HOLDS NEAR $104, DECOUPLING FROM THE EQUITY AND GOLD ROUT
stories.body: WTI crude was little changed, up about 0.92% to roughly $104 a barrel, essentially sitting out the broader risk-asset selloff that hit stocks and gold alike. Steady supply conditions and OPEC+ discipline are keeping oil anchored even as other markets reprice AI-capex risk.
stories.explain: Oil's price is driven primarily by physical supply-and-demand fundamentals — inventories, OPEC+ output quotas, refinery runs — rather than by the equity-market narrative about AI spending, so it has little reason to move just because tech earnings disappoint. That decoupling is itself informative: when a selloff doesn't spread into commodities tied to the real economy, it signals a sector-specific valuation unwind rather than a broader recession scare, which would typically hit oil demand expectations too.

stories.headline: DOLLAR FIRMS TO 101.88 ON DXY, ADDING A THIRD LEG TO THE RISK-OFF COMPLEX
stories.body: The dollar index rose 0.11% to 101.88, extending its advance as capital rotated out of risk assets and into dollar-denominated safety alongside Treasuries. A firmer dollar is itself a modest headwind for gold priced in dollars, compounding the forced-selling pressure on the metal.
stories.explain: The dollar tends to strengthen in a global risk-off episode because it remains the world's primary funding and reserve currency — investors and institutions unwinding leveraged positions need dollars to repay dollar-denominated liabilities, which mechanically bids the currency up. That dollar strength then feeds back into gold, which is priced in dollars, so a stronger greenback makes gold costlier for foreign buyers even before accounting for the liquidation pressure described above.

stories.headline: DIVISION I SEASON TIPS OFF MONDAY WITH NO. 1 FLORIDA HOSTING MIAMI, REIGNING CHAMP MICHIGAN ON THE ROAD
stories.body: Preseason No. 1 Florida opens its title defense bid Monday at 6 p.m. ET against Miami in Tampa, while reigning national champion Michigan — unranked inside the top 15 after Dusty May left for SMU — tips off on the road. Washington's own opener comes the same night against Colgate at Alaska Airlines Arena, and the Champions Classic doubleheader (Duke-Michigan State, Kansas-Kentucky) follows Nov. 10 in Chicago.

stories.headline: WEMBANYAMA POURS IN 43 AS SPURS ROUT TIMBERWOLVES FOR FOURTH STRAIGHT WIN
stories.body: San Antonio's Victor Wembanyama scored 43 points with six blocks and seven rebounds in a 121-111 win over Minnesota, extending the Spurs' winning streak to four games and keeping him squarely in the early MVP conversation. Elsewhere Sunday, Memphis improved to a league-best 6-0 with a 136-105 rout of Sacramento.

stories.headline: COLTS, SEAHAWKS STILL TALKING JONATHAN TAYLOR, BUT SEATTLE'S $3.8M IN CAP SPACE CLOUDS A DEAL
stories.body: Indianapolis remains open to moving its All-Pro back with the Nov. 10, 4 p.m. ET deadline approaching, and Seattle is among the teams that have checked in — but the Seahawks have just $3.8 million in cap room after the Nelson trade and the Christian Haynes waiver, complicating any realistic offer. Seattle hosts Chicago on Monday Night Football looking to stay alone in second place in the NFC West.

stories.headline: UNRANKED USC STUNS NO. 2 OHIO STATE 30-18 AS TRUE FRESHMAN FAHEY'S DEBUT FALLS SHORT
stories.body: True freshman Luke Fahey went 21-of-38 for 260 yards and a touchdown to Jeremiah Smith in his first career start, but Ohio State settled for four field goals and a 2-of-10 red-zone clip in the 30-18 loss at the Coliseum — the week's biggest upset. The result drops the Buckeyes outside the top 10 ahead of Tuesday's first College Football Playoff rankings, the same weekend Indiana beat Minnesota in overtime on dueling 60-yard field goals.

sports.detail: Chris Lawson's 25-yard go-ahead touchdown catch with 1:30 left and Alex McLaughlin's 48-yard pick-six off Anthony Colandrea's third interception sealed it; both teams finish 5-3 (2-3 Big Ten). Next: Saturday vs. Penn State at Husky Stadium.

Danny Sprinkle's Year 3 roster, with nine newcomers filling out all 15 scholarship spots, tips off the regular season Monday at Alaska Airlines Arena chasing the program's first NCAA tournament bid since 2019.

deepDive.title: Why $3.8 Million Changes Everything: The NFL Salary Cap as a Balance-Sheet Constraint
content: Seattle wants Jonathan Taylor, Indianapolis is willing to deal him, and the two sides are reportedly talking — yet the single biggest obstacle isn't draft-pick value, it's a number: $3.8 million in Seahawks cap space. Unlike the NBA's trade exceptions and luxury-tax aprons, which give teams some room to absorb a bigger contract mid-transaction, the NFL's hard cap requires a team's total cap charges to fit under the league limit at the instant a trade is processed — no grace period, no partial credit. That makes a trade for an All-Pro running back less a scouting decision than a balance-sheet problem, and it's the same mechanical constraint quietly shaping every other rumored deal around the league this week.

The mechanism is straightforward bookkeeping, but it's unforgiving. Every player's cap charge is his current-year salary plus the prorated share of any signing bonus; when a team trades for a player, it inherits that full charge immediately, and the acquiring team's cap room must absorb it the moment the trade is official. Seattle's $3.8 million is what's left after absorbing the cap hit from trading for guard Quenton Nelson and the dead money from waiving running back Christian Haynes — commitments that already exist on the books and can't be waved away. There is no 'we'll figure it out after the season' in-season; the room has to exist today.

What most fans miss is that teams can defer cap pain, but never eliminate it — restructuring is refinancing, not forgiveness. Converting a player's base salary into a signing bonus lets a team prorate that money over the remaining years of his contract, shrinking this year's charge while inflating future years' obligations and dead-cap exposure if he's later cut or traded. The New Orleans Saints became the league's cautionary tale for this over the 2010s, repeatedly restructuring veteran deals to stay competitive in the short term until the accumulated future charges made their cap sheet nearly unmanageable for years afterward.

Read against tonight's brief, the parallel to this week's AI-capex selloff is almost exact: both are stories about commitments made today constraining flexibility tomorrow, whether that's a hyperscaler's multi-year capex budget or a cornerback's prorated bonus. For Seattle, acquiring Taylor almost certainly requires a correlated move — a cut, a restructure, or outgoing salary in the same trade — before the Nov. 10 deadline, not just draft-capital horse-trading. The lesson for a finance student watching trade rumors: the interesting number is never just willingness to deal, it's whether the balance sheet actually has room, and that's knowable in advance if you bother to check the cap sheet.
